colleges.name: University of Pennsylvania
colleges.appliesVia: Common App, Coalition App, or Questbridge
colleges.wants: Penn reads writing to see how you think, what you value and how you see the world. Its short answers are meant to show how you consider other people, how you approach community, what drives your academic goals and why Penn in particular. It wants responses that sound recognisably like you rather than a recap of the application.
colleges.notes: Page heading reads '2026-27 Short Answer and Essay Prompts'. Transfer-only essay on the same page was left out (first-year scope).

colleges.name: Columbia University
colleges.appliesVia: Common Application, Coalition Application on Scoir, or QuestBridge Application (QuestBridge Finalists)
colleges.wants: Columbia uses its own questions to gauge intellectual curiosity, habits of mind, love of learning and sense of self, plus who you are in your current community and why Columbia's experience suits you. Across the application it looks for academic preparation, curiosity, engagement with others, an authentic individual voice and real knowledge of Columbia.
colleges.notes: Questions page is headed '2026-2027 Columbia-Specific Questions' and marked 'Updated Tuesday, July 28, 2026'. The 'Understanding the Process' page carries no cycle year (live page, footer 2026). Applies to Columbia College and Columbia Engineering first-year applicants.

colleges.name: University of Chicago
colleges.appliesVia: Apply Coalition, Powered by Scoir or the Common Application (both include the University of Chicago Supplement); a QuestBridge page is also listed
colleges.wants: UChicago says no single element decides fit; it wants the application to show who you really are, in your own voice, not what you imagine it wants to see. Its essay questions are a chance to reveal your tastes and ambitions, and may be answered seriously, playfully or anywhere in between.
colleges.notes: Essay page says 'Introducing the 2026-2027 essay prompts.' The Apply page shows deadlines of Nov 2, 2026 and Jan 4, 2027. UChicago has no dedicated 'what we look for' page that I could find; wants is drawn from the Apply page and the Essay Questions page intro.

colleges.name: Common App
colleges.wants: The essay is where you tell readers what you want them to know about you beyond courses, grades and test scores: who you are and what matters to you, adding something the rest of the application does not show.
colleges.notes: Purpose statement from Common App's 'Telling your story: How to approach the essay' PDF (dated September 2026). Prompts page is labelled 2026-2027.

colleges.name: University of California
colleges.wants: UC wants to hear your personality, background, interests and achievements in your own voice. No question is favoured and there is no right answer; responses add context alongside many other factors and never decide admission alone.
colleges.notes: Live current-cycle page; no cycle year printed on it. Applies to all nine undergraduate campuses.

colleges.name: UC Berkeley
colleges.wants: Holistic review of all academic and personal information, with no single item weighted above another; seeks applicants most likely to contribute to Berkeley's intellectual and cultural community and beyond.
colleges.notes: Live current-cycle page; no cycle year printed on it. UC's link admissions.berkeley.edu/selectsstudents redirects to this URL.

colleges.name: UC Davis
colleges.wants: Reviews every application comprehensively on the 13 shared UC criteria, looking past numbers to academics, extracurricular achievement and responses to life challenges; advises choosing a major you genuinely want.
colleges.notes: Read through the WebFetch tool only (it returns a model summary, not raw text; direct download got HTTP 403). Page shows last-updated July 29, 2026, no cycle year. Marked unverified: the page text itself could not be read.

colleges.name: UC Irvine
colleges.wants: Comprehensive review of A-G coursework, academic achievement, activities, talents and skills, all read in the context of your circumstances and experiences, including your personal insight answers. Grades matter but are not everything.
colleges.notes: Live current-cycle page; no cycle year printed on it. Footer copyright reads 2023.

colleges.name: UCLA
colleges.wants: Seeks intellectual curiosity, tenacity and commitment to community service; readers weigh achievement, personal qualities and likely campus contribution in context of opportunities and challenges. The individual should come through in the PIQs.
colleges.notes: Live current-cycle page; no cycle year printed on it.

colleges.name: University of Washington (Seattle)
colleges.wants: UW treats the essay as its chance to meet the person behind grades and numbers. Academic preparation and performance come first in review, alongside personal achievements and traits such as service, leadership, real responsibility and distinctive perspectives. It wants original writing in the applicant's own voice.
colleges.notes: First-year applicants no longer write a UW-specific essay; the required essay is the Common App personal essay. Application route confirmed at https://admit.washington.edu/apply/first-year/how-to-apply/ (UW does not consider recommendation letters, interviews or demonstrated interest). promptsFrom value 'common-app' is a suggested key, not from the page.

colleges.name: Penn State (University Park)
colleges.appliesVia: MyPennState application or Common App (no preference between them)
colleges.wants: Penn State weighs the academic record most heavily: courses, grades and course levels from grades 9-11, plus test scores if submitted. The optional personal statement and activities list can be additional factors, and reviewers consider the roles an applicant fills as student, family member, athlete, volunteer or employee.
colleges.notes: Personal Statement is optional; Common App Essay is accepted as the Personal Statement. No official Penn State essay-advice page was found, so no principles are included. 'No preference' statement seen at https://www.psu.edu/admission/undergraduate/how-to-apply. Pages are live with 2026 dates (Early Action grace period to November 5, 2026). Linked to the Common App prompts because Penn State accepts the Common App essay as its optional Personal Statement. The MyPennState wording is not published on public pages.

prompts.label: Thank-you note
prompts.text: Write a short thank-you note to someone you have not yet thanked and would like to acknowledge. (We encourage you to share this note with that person, if possible, and reflect on the experience!)
prompts.instructions: Required for all applicants. 50-200 words.
prompts.notes: Word-count parenthetical '(50-200 words)' removed from text and stored in minWords/wordLimit.

prompts.label: Community at Penn
prompts.text: How will you explore community at Penn? Consider how Penn will help shape your perspective, and how your experiences and perspective will help shape Penn.
prompts.instructions: Required for all applicants. 50-200 words.

prompts.label: School-specific: Nursing
prompts.text: Penn Nursing intends to meet the health needs of society in a global and multicultural world by preparing its students to impact healthcare by advancing science. Why are you applying to Nursing, where do you see yourself professionally in the future, and how will you contribute to our mission of promoting equity in healthcare?
prompts.instructions: School-specific: required for applicants whose single-degree school choice is the School of Nursing. 50-200 words.
prompts.notes: Page adds a suggestion to review Penn Nursing's mission and approach to equity in healthcare.

prompts.label: School-specific: College of Arts and Sciences
prompts.text: The College of Arts and Sciences is designed to foster discovery and connection. Describe something you are curious about—something you'd like to learn more about or find a new approach to—and how you might pursue that curiosity in the College.
prompts.instructions: School-specific: required for applicants whose single-degree school choice is the College of Arts and Sciences. 50 to 200 words.
prompts.notes: Page adds a suggestion to look at the College's curriculum and academic offerings.

prompts.label: School-specific: Wharton
prompts.text: Wharton prepares its students to make an impact by applying business methods and economic theory to real-world problems, including economic, political, and social issues. Discuss a current issue of importance to you and how you hope a Wharton education would help you explore it.
prompts.instructions: School-specific: required for applicants whose single-degree school choice is The Wharton School. 50-200 words.
prompts.notes: Page adds a suggestion to review the foundations of a Wharton education.

prompts.label: School-specific: Penn Engineering
prompts.text: Penn Engineering prepares its students to become leaders in technology by combining a strong foundation in the natural sciences and mathematics with depth of study in focused disciplinary majors. Describe how you plan to pursue your engineering interests at Penn, particularly within the intended major you selected.
prompts.instructions: School-specific: required for applicants whose single-degree school choice is Penn Engineering. 50-200 words.
prompts.notes: Page adds a suggestion to review Penn Engineering's mission and the curriculum for the intended major.

prompts.label: Huntsman: target language selection
prompts.text: Applicants to the Huntsman Program in International Studies and Business must choose one of eleven target languages. Please select your target language.
prompts.instructions: Program-specific: Huntsman Program applicants only. A selection, not an essay; no limit given. One of three Huntsman-specific responses, in addition to the two prompts for all applicants.

prompts.label: Huntsman: target language experience
prompts.text: Describe your experience with the target language you selected. You may wish to share the length of time you’ve studied or used this language, how you’ve learned it, the skills you’ve acquired, and/or the skills you still wish to develop. Please also explain why you are interested in studying this language and the region(s) of the world where it is spoken.
prompts.instructions: Program-specific: Huntsman Program applicants only. 50-200 words.

prompts.label: Huntsman: international studies and business
prompts.text: The Huntsman Program supports the development of globally-minded scholars who become engaged citizens, creative innovators, and ethical leaders in the public, private, and non-profit sectors in the United States and around the world. What draws you to a dual degree in international studies and business, and how would you use what you learn to address a global issue where these two domains intersect?
prompts.instructions: Program-specific: Huntsman Program applicants only. 50-400 words.

prompts.label: LSM: Life Sciences and Management
prompts.text: The Vagelos Life Sciences & Management (LSM) program brings together two powerful modes of understanding—scientific inquiry and strategic thinking—to prepare students to engage thoughtfully and creatively with some of the most complex challenges of our time. What questions, problems, or opportunities would you hope to explore through LSM, and how might the integration of life sciences and management shape your approach to them? Focus on the ideas, values, or questions that draw you to this intersection, rather than how LSM might advance your career, and make sure this essay is distinct from your single-degree application.
prompts.instructions: Program-specific: LSM applicants only (one LSM-specific response, in addition to the two prompts for all applicants). 50-400 words.

prompts.label: M&T: engineering and business problems
prompts.text: Explain how you will use the M&T program to pursue problems or opportunities that require both engineering and business perspectives.
prompts.instructions: Program-specific: M&T (Jerome Fisher Program in Management and Technology) applicants only. 50-400 words. One of two M&T-specific responses.

prompts.label: M&T: something you built
prompts.text: Describe something you created, designed, improved, or built. What motivated you, and what did you learn from the process?
prompts.instructions: Program-specific: M&T applicants only. 50-200 words.

prompts.label: NHCM: Nursing and Healthcare Management
prompts.text: Describe your interest in nursing and health care management, and how Penn's coordinated dual-degree program in nursing and business would help you meet your goals. Please ensure that this essay is distinct from your single-degree application, if applicable.
prompts.instructions: Program-specific: NHCM applicants only (one NHCM-specific response, in addition to the two prompts for all applicants). 50 to 400 words.

prompts.label: VIPER: major combination
prompts.text: VIPER students pursue dual degrees in science or math and engineering. Which major combination(s) interest you most right now and why? Your response to this prompt is not binding; students often shift majors as they learn more through the program. See available VIPER majors on our website.
prompts.instructions: Program-specific: VIPER applicants only. 50-200 words. One of two VIPER-specific responses.
prompts.notes: Double spaces between sentences on the page collapsed to single spaces.

prompts.label: VIPER: interest in energy research
prompts.text: Describe your interest in the VIPER program, including how any past experiences (academic, research, extracurricular, etc.) have shaped your interest in energy science and technology, and how you envision participation in VIPER fitting into your future goals.
prompts.instructions: Program-specific: VIPER applicants only. 50-400 words.

prompts.label: VIC: Visual and Interactive Computing
prompts.text: Discuss how your interests align with the Visual and Interactive Computing (VIC) program at the University of Pennsylvania
prompts.instructions: Program-specific: applicants to the BSE in Visual and Interactive Computing only (one VIC-specific response, in addition to the two prompts for all applicants). 50-400 words.
prompts.notes: On the page the sentence ends '... University of Pennsylvania (50-400 words).' with the full stop after the word-count parenthetical.

prompts.label: List: texts, resources and outlets
prompts.text: List the titles of texts, resources and outlets that have contributed to your intellectual development outside of academic courses, including but not limited to books, journals, websites, podcasts, essays, plays, presentations, videos, museums and other content that you enjoy.
prompts.instructions: Required. List question, 100 words or fewer. Give items separated by commas or semicolons; no numbering or particular order needed; no italics or underlining of titles; no author names, subtitles or explanatory remarks.
prompts.notes: Word-limit parenthetical removed from text. Formatting guidance in instructions is paraphrased from the page.

prompts.label: Lived experience
prompts.text: Tell us about an aspect of your life so far or your lived experience that is important to you, and describe how it has shaped the way you would learn from and contribute to Columbia's multidimensional and collaborative environment.
prompts.instructions: Required. Short answer, 150 words or fewer.

prompts.label: Disagreement
prompts.text: At Columbia, students representing a wide range of perspectives are invited to live and learn together. In such a community, questions and debates naturally arise. Please describe a time when you did not agree with someone and discuss how you engaged with them and what you took away from the interaction.
prompts.instructions: Required. Short answer, 150 words or fewer.

prompts.label: Navigating adversity
prompts.text: In college/university, students are often challenged in ways that they could not anticipate. Please describe a situation in which you have navigated through adversity and discuss how you changed as a result.
prompts.instructions: Required. Short answer, 150 words or fewer.

prompts.label: Why Columbia
prompts.text: Why are you interested in attending Columbia University? We encourage you to consider the aspect(s) that you find unique and compelling about Columbia.
prompts.instructions: Required. Short answer, 150 words or fewer.

prompts.label: Preferred areas of study
prompts.text: What attracts you to your preferred areas of study at Columbia College or Columbia Engineering?
prompts.instructions: Required. Short answer, 150 words or fewer.
prompts.notes: The page's instructions refer to 'six short answer questions', but the page lists one list question plus five short answers (six questions in total). All six are recorded here.

prompts.label: Why UChicago
prompts.text: How does the University of Chicago, as you know it now, satisfy your desire for a particular kind of learning, community, and future? Please address with some specificity your own wishes and how they relate to UChicago.
prompts.instructions: Question 1 (Required). No strict word limit; UChicago's FAQ gives 300-600 words as a rough benchmark, not a requirement.
prompts.notes: Length guidance is from https://collegeadmissions.uchicago.edu/apply/uchicago-admissions-faq/ (no cycle year on that page). The older URL /apply/uchicago-supplemental-essay-questions redirects to /apply/essay/.

prompts.label: Extended essay: Food for thought
prompts.text: Food for thought: How do thoughts eat?
prompts.instructions: Question 2: Extended Essay (Required; Choose one). No strict word limit; the FAQ gives 500-700 words as a rough benchmark, not a requirement.
prompts.notes: Attribution on page: Inspired by Ernest Leong, Class of 2026.

prompts.label: Extended essay: Artistic practice as solution
prompts.text: The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, utilized origami-inspired techniques to compactly store and deploy its sunshield in space. Choose an artistic practice and use its principles to propose an elegant solution to a problem.
prompts.instructions: Question 2: Extended Essay (Required; Choose one). No strict word limit; the FAQ gives 500-700 words as a rough benchmark, not a requirement.
prompts.notes: Attribution on page: Inspired by Akhil Korra, Class of 2028.

prompts.label: Extended essay: Mixed metaphor
prompts.text: Sometimes metaphors get mixed up. For one reason or another, one could say, “we'll burn that bridge when we get there” or “the world is your china shop”. Make up your own mixed metaphor. Explain how it could make sense, be understood, or even applied.
prompts.instructions: Question 2: Extended Essay (Required; Choose one). No strict word limit; the FAQ gives 500-700 words as a rough benchmark, not a requirement.
prompts.notes: Attribution on page: Inspired by Julia Nieberg, Class of 2029.

prompts.label: Extended essay: Mundane Olympic event
prompts.text: The Olympics have long celebrated the pinnacle of human athletic achievement. But what if they expanded to honor the mundane? Imagine a new Olympic event built around an everyday activity like speed dishwashing or competitive grocery bagging. How is it scored, officiated, and judged? Why is it a worthy addition?
prompts.instructions: Question 2: Extended Essay (Required; Choose one). No strict word limit; the FAQ gives 500-700 words as a rough benchmark, not a requirement.
prompts.notes: Attribution on page: Inspired by Ewan Smith, Class of 2028.

prompts.label: Extended essay: Mistaken Identity of Acronym
prompts.text: AI: Allen Iverson. NASA, or the North American Saxophone Alliance. Share a potentially confounding, comedic, or captivating example of MIA (Mistaken Identity of Acronym) and tell us its backstory.
prompts.instructions: Question 2: Extended Essay (Required; Choose one). No strict word limit; the FAQ gives 500-700 words as a rough benchmark, not a requirement.
prompts.notes: Attribution on page: Inspired by Jeeho Byun, Class of 2030.

prompts.label: Extended essay: Choose your own adventure
prompts.text: And, as always… the classic choose your own adventure option! In the spirit of adventurous inquiry, choose one of our past prompts (or create a question of your own). Be original, creative, thought provoking. Draw on your best qualities as a writer, thinker, visionary, social critic, sage, citizen of the world, or future citizen of the University of Chicago; take a little risk, and have fun!
prompts.instructions: Question 2: Extended Essay (Required; Choose one). No strict word limit; the FAQ gives 500-700 words as a rough benchmark, not a requirement.
prompts.notes: The same page lists a long 'Past Essay Prompts' archive that this option refers to; the archive is not included here.

rubrics.title: Penn comprehensive review: questions the committee asks

criteria.name: Learner
criteria.description: What your high school courses and academic experiences reveal about how you learn.

criteria.name: Interests and time
criteria.description: What interests you and where you have put your time and energy outside class.

criteria.name: Joy and inspiration
criteria.description: What sustains you or brings you joy, and who or what inspires you.

criteria.name: Context

criteria.name: Academic preparation

criteria.name: Curiosity

principles.text: Read each prompt closely and answer exactly what it asks; an indirect answer leaves the committee deciding with incomplete information.
If you reuse material written for another school, reread it to confirm it genuinely fits this prompt.
Be specific about why Penn: name the classes, research, groups or clubs you would actually pursue there.
Do not summarise the rest of your application; write so that someone who knows you would recognise it as yours without your name.
Aim to convey your real personality, perspectives and motivations so readers understand what makes you tick.
Show you understand what is distinctive about Columbia, such as the Core Curriculum or its urban campus, and why it suits you.
For the list question, give bare titles separated by commas or semicolons: no numbering, authors, subtitles, formatting or explanations.
Whatever tools or support you use, everything submitted must be your own original work in your authentic voice.
Be yourself and write in your own voice, rather than guessing what the admissions office wants to see.
The essay questions can be answered with total seriousness, pure whimsy or something between; take a small risk and enjoy it.
Ideas matter more than word count: the supplement has no strict limits, only rough length benchmarks.
Proofread and edit, and ask someone you trust to read your personal statement before you submit.
Write what you actually want to share about yourself, not what you guess colleges want to hear.
Give readers something new: check that the essay adds information not already found elsewhere in your application.
Choose a topic that reveals who you are and what matters to you.
Small, everyday experiences are valid material when they had a powerful effect on you.
Do not list accomplishments; develop one topic with specific, concrete examples that support your point.
Write in the first person, using 'I' and 'my', so readers get to know you.
There is no right answer; use your own voice to show your personality, background, interests and achievements.
Start early and leave time to prepare, compose carefully and revise.
Proofread for clarity; grammar is not graded, but errors distract readers from what you mean.
Seek feedback from people you trust, but the ideas and every word must be your own.
Treat the essay seriously: write in formal, standard English rather than the casual style of a text message.
Tell a personal story in your own individual voice; many of the strongest statements take that form.
Keep the writing concise and straightforward, and proofread it repeatedly before submitting.
The writing must be your own original work; any review by a person or AI tool has to be responsible and ethical.
